name: Nettle root

lead: Nettle root is the root of the stinging nettle, with extracts long used in European herbal products for benign prostatic hyperplasia. In supplement circles it is taken to bind SHBG so more testosterone stays free, for better training results and a leaner look.

Lab studies report that components of the root bind SHBG, though Grokipedia says the clinical significance is unclear. A 12-month randomised trial of a root extract in 246 BPH patients reported symptom improvement over placebo; no human trial tests it for testosterone or appearance.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or extract, often in stacks with other testosterone-support supplements. Users generally take it for weeks to months alongside training and judge by bloodwork and gym progress.

Grokipedia, an AI-generated and therefore unverified source, reports rare mild digestive upset, advises against oral use in pregnancy and lists possible interactions with diuretics, blood-pressure and diabetes drugs, lithium and warfarin.

chain: Extract binds SHBG in the lab
angle.text: Nettle root extract is taken to bind SHBG, leaving more free testosterone for muscle and a leaner look. Trials have studied it for prostate symptoms; the testosterone link comes from lab work.

lead: Nettle root refers to extracts of the roots of Urtica dioica, the common stinging nettle. Root extracts have a long tradition in German phytotherapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia [1].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding supplement discussions, nettle root is promoted as an SHBG binder, based on laboratory work showing that certain root constituents bind SHBG [2][3]. Grokipedia states that the clinical significance of this for testosterone is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence [2].

The human evidence that exists concerns urinary symptoms of BPH. A 12-month randomised, placebo-controlled trial of a nettle root extract in 246 patients reported a statistically significant improvement in symptom score compared with placebo [1].
infobox: Sold as a herbal / dietary supplement

paras: SHBG is a blood protein that binds sex hormones. Proponents say that a nettle root compound occupying SHBG leaves more testosterone unbound. Laboratory studies reported that lignans from the root, including one with high affinity, bind human SHBG, and that aqueous root extracts inhibit SHBG binding to prostate membranes [2]. A 2020 biochemical study examined interactions between SHBG and nonsteroidal ligands that enhance androgen activity [3].

Other laboratory studies examined root extracts on prostate cell lines, reporting an antiproliferative effect on LNCaP cancer cells [4], inhibition of enzyme activity in BPH tissue [5] and inhibition of induced prostate growth in mice [6]. A 2024 study tested a combined saw palmetto and nettle root extract on prostate hyperplasia and inflammation in rats and human cells [7].
No studies found that test nettle root for testosterone, free testosterone or appearance outcomes.

For BPH, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of 459 mg of dry nettle root extract (Bazoton-uno) enrolled 246 patients for one year; the International Prostate Symptom Score fell from 18.7 to 13.0 on the extract versus 18.5 to 13.8 on placebo (p=0.0233) [1]. Grokipedia also cites a systematic review of randomised trials reporting improved symptom scores with Urtica extracts and no significant adverse effects versus controls, without giving its year [2].

Grokipedia reports that oral use is generally considered safe up to a year at recommended doses with rare mild gastrointestinal effects, that oral preparations are contraindicated in pregnancy, and that possible interactions include diuretics, antidiabetic and blood-pressure drugs, lithium and warfarin [2]. These statements are from an AI-generated source and are not independently verified here.
